sections.section_title: Iconium -- The Pattern Repeats and Intensifies
sections.summary: Paul and Barnabas preach in the Iconium synagogue, producing a large number of Jewish and Greek believers, while 'the disobedient Jews' (hoi apeithesantes) willfully refuse the message and stir up opposition, and the Lord confirms the word of his grace with signs and wonders.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading identifies the verb apeitheo as carrying 'the connotation of willful refusal' -- these are 'not Jews who failed to understand' but 'Jews who rejected the message.' This frames unbelief as a deliberate human choice rather than a divinely determined outcome. Correspondingly, the 'large number' who believed did so in response to the missionaries' speaking, presenting faith as the human side of a dynamic in which God confirms but humans respond.
key_phrases: spoke in such a way that a large number of people believed
hoi apeithesantes -- the Jews who refused to be persuaded
the Lord, who was testifying to the word of His grace

sections.section_title: Division, Threat, and Flight to Lycaonia
sections.summary: The city of Iconium divides over the missionaries, a plot to stone them forms involving both Jews and Gentile rulers, and Paul and Barnabas flee to Lycaonia where they continue preaching.

sections.section_title: A Lame Man Healed at Lystra
sections.summary: A man lame from birth listens to Paul's preaching at Lystra, and Paul perceives that the man has 'faith to be made well' (pistin tou sothenai) -- a response to hearing the gospel that results in his dramatic healing.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading notes that the man 'heard the gospel; he responded with faith; that faith included but was not limited to the expectation of physical restoration.' Faith is presented as a human response to the proclaimed word -- the man listened, and from that listening arose faith. The verb sozo carries both physical and spiritual dimensions, and the man's faith is portrayed as his own response rather than something imposed on him. The pattern is: word proclaimed, word heard, faith arises in the hearer, divine power acts on the basis of that faith.
key_phrases: this man was listening to Paul as he spoke
Paul saw that he had faith

sections.section_title: The Crowd's Pagan Response -- Zeus and Hermes
sections.summary: The Lycaonian crowd interprets the healing through their pagan mythological framework, identifies Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes, and the priest of Zeus prepares a formal civic sacrifice.

sections.section_title: Paul's Speech to Pagans -- The Living God Who Made Everything
sections.summary: Paul and Barnabas reject worship, declaring themselves mere humans who preach the gospel so that the Lycaonians will 'turn from these useless things to a living God' who made everything, who permitted the nations to go their own ways in past generations but always provided witness through creation.
sections.relevance: The gospel call to pagans is framed as an invitation to 'turn' (epistrephein) -- a verb that presupposes the audience's capacity and responsibility to reorient themselves. The neutral reading notes this parallels Acts 17:30 where God 'commands all people everywhere to repent,' signaling that the era of divine patience has ended and a universal human response is now expected. God's past 'permitting' the nations to go their own ways (eiasen) implies that wandering was the nations' own action, not divinely imposed, and the present call to turn implies the turning is likewise theirs to perform.
key_phrases: to turn from these useless things to a living God
He permitted all the nations to go their own ways
He did not leave Himself without witness

sections.summary: Jews from Antioch and Iconium persuade the Lycaonian crowd to stone Paul; he is dragged out of the city and left for dead, but rises when the disciples gather around him and enters the city, departing for Derbe the next day.

sections.section_title: The Return Journey -- Strengthening, Exhorting, Organizing
sections.summary: Paul and Barnabas retrace their route through hostile cities, strengthening the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, teaching that entrance to the kingdom requires enduring many tribulations, and appointing elders in every church before entrusting the communities to the Lord.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading draws the explicit inference: 'The exhortation to continue presupposes that continuance is not automatic. If perseverance were guaranteed, the exhortation would be pointless. The fact that Paul urges these new believers to continue in the faith implies that not continuing is a real possibility.' The kingdom of God is presented as something to be 'entered' (eiselthein) through a path of many tribulations, framing salvation's consummation as requiring sustained human faithfulness. This is the author's own argument -- not an aside or illustration -- about the structure of the Christian life: initial faith must become ongoing commitment, and the believers' own perseverance through tribulation is the path by which they reach the kingdom.
key_phrases: encouraging them to continue in the faith
it is through many tribulations that we must enter the kingdom of God
entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had believed

sections.section_title: The Return to Antioch -- Report to the Sending Church
sections.summary: Paul and Barnabas preach in Perga on the return journey, sail to Antioch in Syria, and report to the sending church that God had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
sections.relevance: The summary statement 'God opened a door of faith to the Gentiles' attributes initiative to God while using a metaphor that inherently requires human response. The neutral reading states: 'God opened a door and the Gentiles walked through it.' A door opened is an invitation and an opportunity, not a forced passage. God's action creates access; the Gentiles' faith is their walking through. The passage presents divine initiative and human response as complementary rather than presenting God as unilaterally determining who believes.
key_phrases: all the things that God had done with them
He had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles
